content.content:
# Container Environment Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it tries.

### Shape

#### Description

Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps, and questions from the Ask tab always run in a container. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step run in one only while the project's "Run code tasks in a container" option is on, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says; while it is off, they run on the host as ever, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, with its protected locations. Freeform tasks always run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles, which change nothing.
Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes commits there, as ever.

#### Runtime

The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command, and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.
On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

#### Missing Podman

Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task, a Chain prompt's steps, a question, and, while the project's option is on, a Code task. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed does, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, or as one whose spec build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

- on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
- on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
- on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

While the project's option is off, a Code task never needs Podman, and runs whether it is installed or not.

#### Podman Machine

On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`. Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

#### Podman Access

Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed. The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written, what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead. The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that the build failed.

#### Image

Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`, and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions changes.
A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own, `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add the toolchains its code needs, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the project's runs use the default image.
While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

#### Mounts

What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing else from the host. Each is mounted at the same absolute path it has on the host, where the platform allows it, so the paths the harness reports in what it does need no mapping, and the run works in the project directory's path, as a run on the host does. What each kind of run is given, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) names the locations:

##### Spec

A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location.

##### Question

A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only. Never the spec location. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volumes.

##### Code

A Code task, or a Chain prompt's code step, while the project's option is on: the code location, read and write; the compiled reference and piton.config.pi, read only; the task's understanding file, read and write; and the project's caches. Never the spec location.

Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it.
A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not written yet is.

#### Paths

Where a mount can't be at the host's path, as on macOS and Windows, where the container sees the project at a path of its own, every path a run reports from its container is mapped back to its host path before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls touched. A path that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and opens nothing.

#### Volumes

What a harness keeps between runs is kept in Podman volumes the application owns and names, never in the project:

- one per harness, for its login and settings, ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness keeps it, shared by every project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them
- one per project and conversation, the spec lane's, the code lane's, and the questions', for the harness's sessions, so each carries on its own conversation, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says
- the project's caches, such as the cargo registry and target directory, for its Code tasks run in a container

Losing a volume costs only a login or a cache, never anything of the project's.

#### Logging In

When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.

#### Guards

A run in a container has no protected locations, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) names them: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location, since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, name only what it can see. Runs on the host keep their protected locations as ever.

#### Spec Build

A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work in the refreshed reference; with no code location there, what that build writes into the code location, the shape's guidance, goes nowhere. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over, however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as the [SpecBuildScope](../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, so the host's reference and shape guidance are those of the spec as the run left it.
----

.claude/reference/scope/project-data/index.md:30:- `Containerfile`: written by hand, when the project has one, built FROM the application's default image to add what the project's runs need, such as its toolchains, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says

Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps, and questions from the Ask tab always run in a container. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step run in one only while the project's "Run code tasks in a container" option is on, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says; while it is off, they run on the host as ever, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, with its protected locations. Freeform tasks always run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles, which change nothing.
Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes commits there, as ever.

#### Runtime

The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command, and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.
On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

#### Missing Podman

Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task, a Chain prompt's steps, a question, and, while the project's option is on, a Code task. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed does, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, or as one whose spec build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

- on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
- on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
- on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

While the project's option is off, a Code task never needs Podman, and runs whether it is installed or not.

#### Podman Machine

On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`. Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

#### Podman Access

Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed. The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written, what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead. The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that the build failed.

#### Image

Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`, and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions changes.
A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own, `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add the toolchains its code needs, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the project's runs use the default image.
While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

#### Mounts

What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing else from the host. Each is mounted at the same absolute path it has on the host, where the platform allows it, so the paths the harness reports in what it does need no mapping, and the run works in the project directory's path, as a run on the host does. What each kind of run is given, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) names the locations:

##### Spec

A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location.

##### Question

A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only. Never the spec location. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volumes.

##### Code

A Code task, or a Chain prompt's code step, while the project's option is on: the code location, read and write; the compiled reference and piton.config.pi, read only; the task's understanding file, read and write; and the project's caches. Never the spec location.

Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it.
A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not written yet is.

#### Paths

Where a mount can't be at the host's path, as on macOS and Windows, where the container sees the project at a path of its own, every path a run reports from its container is mapped back to its host path before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls touched. A path that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and opens nothing.

#### Volumes

What a harness keeps between runs is kept in Podman volumes the application owns and names, never in the project:

- one per harness, for its login and settings, ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness keeps it, shared by every project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them
- one per project and conversation, the spec lane's, the code lane's, and the questions', for the harness's sessions, so each carries on its own conversation, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says
- the project's caches, such as the cargo registry and target directory, for its Code tasks run in a container

Losing a volume costs only a login or a cache, never anything of the project's.

#### Logging In

When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.

#### Guards

A run in a container has no protected locations, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) names them: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location, since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, name only what it can see. Runs on the host keep their protected locations as ever.

#### Spec Build

A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work in the refreshed reference; with no code location there, what that build writes into the code location, the shape's guidance, goes nowhere. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over, however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as the [SpecBuildScope](../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, so the host's reference and shape guidance are those of the spec as the run left it.

content.text:
Yes, containerized sessions continue across runs, and also after the app restarts. The spec says so (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md`, "Volumes", and `harness-integration/index.md:52-54`), and the code in `src` does it.

**How it works:**
- **Where sessions are stored:** each project has a separate Podman volume for each conversation: one for the spec lane, one for the code lane, and one for Ask questions. The name is `suspense-sessions-<project-key>-<conversation>` (`src/container.rs:355`). Every containerized run mounts it over the harness's session directory in its home (`src/container.rs:303-310`). Containers are run with `--rm`, so the container itself is deleted after each run, but the volume stays.
- **Login:** each harness is logged in once, in a volume shared by every project (`suspense-home-claude` and so on). You don't log in again for each run.
- **Resuming:** the next run in the same lane passes the stored session ID back to the harness (`--resume` for Claude Code, `resume` for Codex, `--session` for OpenCode), so the conversation picks up where it left off.
- **After a restart:** when a project is opened, the latest session ID is read back from the saved prompt history (`Session::latest`, `src/prompt_mode.rs:1979`). That works because the volume still holds the session it points to.

**Limits:**
- **A conversation stays where it began.** A session started on the host can't be resumed in a container, and the reverse doesn't work either. Turning "Run code tasks in a container" on or off makes the code lane start a new conversation at its next task (`src/prompt_mode.rs:6135-6144`). Questions only resume conversations that began in the questions' volume.
- **The container/host flag isn't saved.** Sessions restored from history after a restart have `in_container: None`, so the app tries to resume them either way. If the session ID is somewhere else (for example, it began on the host before the option was switched on), the harness reports "No conversation found". The app then sends the same prompt again straight away as a new conversation, without failing (`src/harness.rs:767`). You lose the earlier context but no work.
- **Deleting volumes loses context.** If the Podman volumes are deleted (for example by `podman volume prune`), the sessions are gone and the next run starts fresh the same way. Project files are never affected.
- **Moving the project changes the volume.** The volume name comes from a project key that appears to be derived from the project directory's path. I didn't confirm this in `project_key`. If it's true, moving or renaming the project directory would point it at a new, empty session volume.
